title: Priests, Libyans and Kushites
subtitle: 1200–664 BC · The End of the New Kingdom, the Divided Kingdom, and the Third Intermediate Period

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From Ramesses III and the Sea Peoples through the split of Egypt between Tanis and Thebes, the Libyan dynasties, and the Kushite pharaohs to the Assyrian sack

entries.label: Setnakhte — order restored after the interregnum
entries.hint: Setnakhte seized the throne at the end of the chaotic close of the Nineteenth Dynasty and founded the Twentieth. His Elephantine stela and, later, the Great Harris Papyrus in his son's name describe the preceding years as anarchy — 'Egypt was in the hands of chiefs and of rulers of towns', a Syrian usurper leading the country to ruin — and himself as the god-sent restorer. He reigned only a few years but stabilised the succession.
entries.note: Elephantine stela of Setnakhte: Drenkhahn, Die Elephantine-Stele des Sethnacht (1980). Great Harris Papyrus (P. BM EA 9999), historical section: Grandet, Le papyrus Harris I (1994). Dodson, Poisoned Legacy: The Fall of the Nineteenth Egyptian Dynasty (2010).

entries.label: Ramesses III — the last great pharaoh
entries.hint: Ramesses III fought off two Libyan invasions and, in his eighth year, the land-and-sea assault of the Sea Peoples, recording all three on the walls of his fortress-temple at Medinet Habu. His reign also saw the first documented labour strike, when the Deir el-Medina workmen downed tools over late rations, and ended with a conspiracy in the royal harem to kill him and put a minor son on the throne — a plot that, a recent CT scan of his mummy shows, cut his throat.
entries.note: Medinet Habu reliefs and texts: Epigraphic Survey, Medinet Habu I–II (1930–32). The strike: Turin Strike Papyrus, W.F. Edgerton, 'The Strikes in Ramses III's Twenty-Ninth Year', JNES 10 (1951). Harem conspiracy: Judicial Papyrus of Turin; throat wound, Hawass et al., BMJ 345 (2012).

entries.label: Ramesses IV to VI — the empire slips away
entries.hint: Ramesses IV mounted one last huge state expedition — over 8,000 men to the Wadi Hammamat quarries — and had a plan of the mining district drawn, the Turin Papyrus map, the oldest surviving geological map. But under him and his successors Egypt lost its hold on the Levant and on Nubia, temple grain-rations to the tomb-workers fell into arrears, and the reign of Ramesses V ended amid unrest and, his mummy suggests, smallpox. The Wilbour Papyrus land register dates from these years.
entries.note: Turin Mining Papyrus: Harrell & Brown, 'The oldest surviving topographical map from ancient Egypt', JARCE 29 (1992). Wadi Hammamat expedition: rock stela of Ramesses IV. Wilbour Papyrus: Gardiner, The Wilbour Papyrus (1941–52). Ramesses V smallpox: Elliot Smith, The Royal Mummies (1912).

entries.label: Ramesses VII to X — grain crisis and the tomb robberies
entries.hint: Through the later Twentieth Dynasty the Theban west bank came apart. Grain prices spiked to several times the old norm during a subsistence crisis, workmen abandoned Deir el-Medina for the safety of the temple enclosures, Libyan raiders threatened the necropolis (the 'year of the hyenas, when one hungered'), and gangs systematically looted the royal and noble tombs — crimes investigated in a series of trials under Ramesses IX whose records survive.
entries.note: Tomb-robbery papyri: Abbott (BM EA 10221), Amherst–Leopold II, Mayer A and B; T. Eric Peet, The Great Tomb-Robberies of the Twentieth Egyptian Dynasty (1930). Grain prices: Janssen, Commodity Prices from the Ramessid Period (1975). Jac. Janssen, 'Absence from Work by the Necropolis Workmen', SAK 8 (1980).

entries.label: Ramesses XI and the end of the New Kingdom
entries.hint: Under the last Ramesses the state stopped functioning as one. The High Priest of Amun, Amenhotep, was besieged and 'suppressed' for months; the viceroy of Kush, Panehsy, marched north to restore order and ended up occupying Thebes and looting it; the generals Herihor and then Piankh took over the south, Herihor taking royal titles at Karnak. A new era-count, the wehem-mesut ('Repeating of Births' or Renaissance), was declared from Year 19. When Ramesses XI died the New Kingdom died with him.
entries.note: The Late Ramesside Letters (Wente, 1967) document the Panehsy war and Piankh's Nubian campaign. Herihor at the Khonsu temple: Epigraphic Survey, The Temple of Khonsu (1979–81). Reconstruction: Kitchen, The Third Intermediate Period in Egypt (3rd ed. 1996) §1–20; Thijs, various GM articles on the chronology.

entries.label: Smendes — the north from Tanis
entries.hint: Smendes, based in the eastern Delta, took the kingship of the whole country in name while in fact ruling only from Memphis northwards; the Theban high priests ran the south. He is the founder of the Twenty-first Dynasty and made Tanis the northern capital, quarrying the abandoned Ramesside city of Pi-Ramesses nearby for its stone. The literary Report of Wenamun, describing an Egyptian envoy humiliated on a timber-buying trip to Byblos, is set in his reign and captures the collapse of Egyptian prestige abroad.
entries.note: Report of Wenamun (Moscow Papyrus 120): Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.224–30. Tanis: Pierre Montet, Les nouvelles fouilles de Tanis (1933) and later; Philippe Brissaud & the Mission Française des Fouilles de Tanis. Kitchen, TIP (1996) §21–30.

entries.label: Psusennes I — the silver pharaoh
entries.hint: Psusennes I reigned about four decades over the north and was buried inside the temple precinct at Tanis in a granite sarcophagus reused from a Ramesside king, holding a coffin of solid silver and a gold mask — a royal burial found undisturbed by Pierre Montet in 1940, on the eve of the German occupation, and almost the equal of Tutankhamun's though far less known. The Tanite kings also held, or shared, the office of High Priest of Amun to bind the two halves of Egypt.
entries.note: Tomb of Psusennes I (NRT III), Tanis: Montet, Les constructions et le tombeau de Psousennès à Tanis (1951). Overview: Henri Stierlin & Christiane Ziegler, Tanis: Trésors des pharaons (1987); Kitchen, TIP (1996) §31–39.

entries.label: Siamun and the last Tanite kings
entries.hint: Siamun was among the more active later kings of the Twenty-first Dynasty, building at Tanis and Memphis; a relief fragment showing him smiting an enemy holding a double axe has been linked, speculatively, to a campaign in Philistia and to the biblical pharaoh who took Gezer and gave it as dowry to Solomon's Egyptian wife. His successor Psusennes II was the last of the line before power passed to the Libyan family of Bubastis.
entries.note: Siamun smiting relief: Montet, Le drame d'Avaris (1941). The Gezer/Solomon question: Kitchen, TIP (1996) §229–31; Paul Ash, David, Solomon and Egypt (1999) is sceptical. Dodson, Afterglow of Empire (2012).

entries.label: Shoshenq I — reunification and the raid on Judah
entries.hint: Shoshenq I, hereditary 'Great Chief of the Meshwesh' — a Libyan military family settled at Bubastis for generations — took the throne and founded the Twenty-second Dynasty. He reasserted real control over Thebes by installing his own son as High Priest of Amun, and mounted a campaign through Palestine, recorded in a long place-name list on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak, generally identified with the 'Shishak' who plundered Jerusalem in the biblical account.
entries.note: Bubastite Portal, Karnak: Epigraphic Survey, Reliefs and Inscriptions at Karnak III: The Bubastite Portal (1954). Megiddo stele fragment of Shoshenq I: Fisher, The Excavation of Armageddon (1929). Biblical account: 1 Kings 14:25–26. Kitchen, TIP (1996) §251–74.

entries.label: Osorkon I and Osorkon II — the dynasty at its height
entries.hint: Osorkon I recorded temple donations of gold and silver on a scale — many tonnes — that only Shoshenq's Levantine plunder can explain, and married into the old Tanite line. Osorkon II built extensively at Bubastis and Tanis, held a great jubilee, and — most likely — sent the Egyptian contingent that fought in the coalition against Assyria at Qarqar in 853. After him the dynasty began to split into rival branches.
entries.note: Osorkon I donation texts: Kitchen, TIP (1996) §275–79. Bubastis jubilee gate of Osorkon II: Édouard Naville, The Festival-Hall of Osorkon II in the Great Temple of Bubastis (1892). Qarqar: the Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III (BM 118884).

entries.label: Prince Osorkon and the Theban civil wars
entries.hint: Prince Osorkon, son of King Takelot II and appointed High Priest of Amun at Thebes, spent much of his life fighting a rival Theban faction for control of the temple and the south. His own account, the 'Chronicle of Prince Osorkon' carved on the Bubastite Portal, records years of expulsion, return, rebellion 'the like of which had not been seen', and the killing and burning of opponents — the fullest narrative of the internal wars that were pulling the Libyan state apart.
entries.note: Chronicle of Prince Osorkon: Ricardo Caminos, The Chronicle of Prince Osorkon (1958). Analysis: Kitchen, TIP (1996) §295–331; Gerard Broekman, 'The Chronological Position of King Takeloth II', in Broekman et al. (eds.), The Libyan Period in Egypt (2009).

entries.label: The many kings — Egypt breaks into chiefdoms
entries.hint: By the later eighth century Egypt had no single ruler. A parallel Twenty-third Dynasty ruled from Leontopolis; 'great chiefs of the Meshwesh' held Mendes, Sebennytos, Busiris and the western Delta as hereditary princedoms; there were kings at Herakleopolis and Hermopolis; and Tefnakht, then Bakenranef, of Sais (the Twenty-fourth Dynasty) were welding the western Delta into the strongest of the fragments. Piye's stela lists about a dozen crowned or chief rulers between the sea and Middle Egypt.
entries.note: The political map: Kitchen, TIP (1996) §III; Robert Morkot, 'Kings and Kingship in Ancient Nubia', in Fisher et al. (eds.), Ancient Nubia (2012). Tefnakht and Sais: the Athens stela and the Piye Victory Stela. Broekman et al. (eds.), The Libyan Period in Egypt (2009).

entries.label: Herihor — the general who ruled Thebes as a king
entries.hint: Herihor combined the offices of army commander, viceroy of Kush and High Priest of Amun, and in the forecourt of the Khonsu temple at Karnak had himself shown with the full royal titulary in a cartouche, facing the god as an equal — while dating documents by the regnal years of Ramesses XI far to the north. He is the point at which Theban Egypt became, in practice, a temple-state ruled by the priesthood of Amun.
entries.note: Khonsu temple forecourt reliefs: Epigraphic Survey, The Temple of Khonsu I (1979). The Herihor/Piankh order of succession is debated (Jansen-Winkeln, 'Das Ende des Neuen Reiches', ZÄS 119, 1992, argues Piankh preceded Herihor). Kitchen, TIP (1996) §1–20.

entries.label: Pinedjem I to Pinedjem II — the priestly dynasty
entries.hint: Herihor's successors ran the Thebaid as a hereditary line, marrying into the Tanite royal house so that the two families were one. Pinedjem I took a full kingly titulary; Menkheperre governed for nearly half a century and walled the Karnak precinct; and under Pinedjem II the priests gathered the plundered, rewrapped bodies of the great New Kingdom pharaohs — Seti I, Ramesses II and the rest — and hid them in two caches, where they lay until the 1870s–1898.
entries.note: The royal caches: DB320 (Deir el-Bahari) and KV35 (tomb of Amenhotep II). Dockets recording the reburials: Kitchen, TIP (1996) §40–58; Nicholas Reeves, Valley of the Kings: The Decline of a Royal Necropolis (1990). Karnak enclosure of Menkheperre.

entries.label: The God's Wife of Amun as ruler of the south
entries.hint: As the High Priesthood's political weight faded, real authority over Thebes and Upper Egypt passed to the God's Wife of Amun — a celibate royal princess, 'married' to the god, who ruled with her own estates, officials and building programme and passed the office on by adopting the next incumbent as daughter. The line runs from Libyan princesses (Karomama) through the Kushite Amenirdis I and Shepenwepet II to the Saite Nitocris, each adoption marking who controlled the south.
entries.note: Mariam Ayad, God's Wife, God's Servant: The God's Wife of Amun (c.740–525 BC) (2009). Chapels of the God's Wives at Medinet Habu. The Nitocris Adoption Stela (Cairo JE 36327), 656 BC, transfers the succession to the Saites.

entries.label: Kashta — Kush reaches into Egypt
entries.hint: The kings of Kush, ruling from Napata below the holy mountain of Gebel Barkal, had absorbed Egyptian religion and script over the centuries the Egyptians were fragmenting. Kashta pushed the Kushite border down to at least Aswan and had his daughter Amenirdis I adopted by the sitting God's Wife of Amun at Thebes as her heir — a bloodless annexation of Upper Egypt by way of its central religious office.
entries.note: Kashta's stela from Elephantine; his name on objects at Thebes. Origins of the Napatan state: László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997); Robert Morkot, The Black Pharaohs: Egypt's Nubian Rulers (2000) pp.139–66.

entries.label: Piye — the conquest of Egypt
entries.hint: When Tefnakht of Sais began uniting the Delta and pushed south, Piye sent his army north and then came himself. His Victory Stela from the temple at Gebel Barkal — one of the longest and most vivid royal narratives from ancient Egypt — describes the sieges of Hermopolis (where he berated the defeated prince for starving his horses) and Memphis, the submission of four rival kings and the Delta chiefs, his scrupulous observance of Egyptian religious purity, and his return upriver with the loot, leaving Egypt nominally his but locally still run by its princes.
entries.note: Piye (Piankhy) Victory Stela (Cairo JE 48862), from Gebel Barkal temple B 500: Grimal, La stèle triomphale de Pi(ankh)y (1981); translation, Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature III (1980) pp.66–84.

entries.label: Shabaka and Shebitku — one kingdom of Egypt and Kush
entries.hint: Shabaka turned Piye's loose overlordship into direct rule: he resided in Egypt, is said to have burned the last Saite king Bakenranef alive, and put his family into the key Theban offices. A slab in his name, the Shabaka Stone, claims to preserve an ancient Memphite text on creation by the god Ptah. His successor Shebitku brought Kushite forces into the Levant, backing Hezekiah of Judah and the coalition against Assyria's westward push.
entries.note: Shabaka Stone (BM EA 498). Burning of Bakenranef: Manetho (Africanus). Shebitku and the 2 Kings 19 / Isaiah 37 'Tirhakah' campaign — the co-regency and dating debated: Frédéric Payraudeau, 'Retour sur la succession Shabaka-Shabataka', NeHeT 1 (2014); Morkot, The Black Pharaohs (2000).

entries.label: Taharqa — the peak and the Assyrian war
entries.hint: Taharqa's early reign was a golden age — exceptionally high Nile floods he read as divine favour, and vast building at Karnak (the great columned kiosk), Kawa, Sanam and Gebel Barkal, plus new pyramids at Nuri. Then Assyria struck: Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 and carried off Taharqa's queen and heir; Taharqa retook it; Ashurbanipal drove him out for good in 667, and he died at Napata two years later, leaving the throne to his nephew Tantamani.
entries.note: Kawa temple inscriptions of Taharqa: M.F.L. Macadam, The Temples of Kawa (1949–55). High Niles: the 'Year 6' Kawa stela. Assyrian campaigns: Esarhaddon's Zincirli and Nahr el-Kalb stelae; Ashurbanipal's Rassam Cylinder. Kahn, 'Taharqa, King of Kush and the Assyrians', JSSEA 31 (2004).

entries.label: Tantamani and the sack of Thebes
entries.hint: Tantamani marched north in 664, retook Memphis and killed the Assyrian vassal Necho I of Sais — a victory told, in the old style, as a prophetic dream on his Dream Stela from Gebel Barkal. Ashurbanipal answered in 663 by sacking Thebes itself, hauling away two obelisks and immense treasure; the fall of 'No-Amon' still shocked the prophet Nahum a generation later. The Kushites withdrew to Napata, and Necho's son Psamtik I, backed by Assyria, took over all Egypt as the Twenty-sixth Dynasty.
entries.note: Dream Stela of Tantamani (Cairo JE 48863), Gebel Barkal: Grimal, Quatre stèles napatéennes (1981). Sack of Thebes: Ashurbanipal's Rassam Cylinder (Prism A); Nahum 3:8–10. Anthony Spalinger, 'The Year 712 B.C. and its Implications for Egyptian History', JARCE 10 (1973) and follow-ups.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Sea Peoples repelled, the Theban civil wars, Shoshenq's raid on Judah, and the Assyrian invasions

entries.label: The Sea Peoples repelled
entries.loc: the eastern Delta frontier / the Nile mouths
entries.hint: In his eighth year Ramesses III met a coalition on the move — Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh, with their families and ox-carts by land and a fleet by sea — that had already destroyed Hatti, Ugarit and Cyprus. Egyptian troops broke the land column near the frontier, and archers on the shore, backed by ships with grapnels, smashed the fleet in the Nile mouths. Egypt held, but the Peleset settled the southern Levantine coast as the Philistines, and the empire there was finished.
entries.note: Medinet Habu, Year 8 reliefs and text: Epigraphic Survey, Medinet Habu I (1930); Papyrus Harris I. Analysis: Eric Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014); Nancy Sandars, The Sea Peoples (1985).

entries.label: Ramesses III's Libyan wars
entries.hint: Ramesses III fought two big Libyan invasions of the western Delta, in his fifth and eleventh years, against the Libu and Meshwesh coming with their herds and households to settle. Medinet Habu records the battles with the usual tallies-of-slaughter tallies — thousands of hands and phalluses counted, chiefs captured. The Egyptians won both, but Libyan groups kept infiltrating and settling, and within two centuries their descendants would supply Egypt's kings.
entries.note: Medinet Habu, Year 5 and Year 11 Libyan war reliefs and texts: Epigraphic Survey, Medinet Habu I–II (1930–32). Libyan settlement and its long consequences: Anthony Leahy (ed.), Libya and Egypt c.1300–750 BC (1990).

entries.label: The war of the High Priest
entries.hint: Late in Ramesses XI's reign the High Priest of Amun, Amenhotep, was driven from office and besieged for months in an episode the texts call the 'suppression'. The viceroy of Kush, Panehsy, brought his army north to intervene, restored the priest, then turned on the Theban authorities and plundered the region before being pushed back into Nubia by the general Piankh, who pursued him upriver. Out of this fighting the military-priestly rulers of the new Thebes emerged.
entries.note: The Late Ramesside Letters, esp. the correspondence of the scribe Dhutmose: Edward Wente, Late Ramesside Letters (1967); Wente, Letters from Ancient Egypt (1990). Kitchen, TIP (1996) §7–15.

entries.label: Shoshenq I's campaign in Palestine
entries.hint: Shoshenq I led an army through Palestine, and a place-name list of more than 150 entries on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak traces routes through Judah, the Negev and the northern kingdom of Israel, including Megiddo, where a fragment of a victory stela in his name was later dug up. The biblical books of Kings remember 'Shishak king of Egypt' in the fifth year of Rehoboam stripping the treasures of the Temple and palace in Jerusalem.
entries.note: Bubastite Portal list: Epigraphic Survey, Reliefs and Inscriptions at Karnak III (1954); Kevin Wilson, The Campaign of Pharaoh Shoshenq I into Palestine (2005). 1 Kings 14:25–28; 2 Chronicles 12.

entries.label: Egypt at the Battle of Qarqar
entries.hint: Shalmaneser III of Assyria, in his sixth year, fought a western coalition on the Orontes: Hadadezer of Damascus, Ahab of Israel, and, among the smaller contingents his monolith inscription lists, '1,000 soldiers of Musri' — most likely a force sent by Osorkon II. It is the first time Egypt appears, even at the margin, on the receiving end of Assyrian expansion, a foretaste of the confrontation that would consume the Kushite dynasty.
entries.note: Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III (BM 118884): translation in ANET pp.278–79. The 'Musri = Egypt' reading: Kitchen, TIP (1996) §284; some scholars prefer a north-Syrian Musri.

entries.label: The wars of Prince Osorkon
entries.hint: For roughly two decades the High Priest Prince Osorkon and a rival Theban faction fought for the temple of Amun and the south, with the Delta king intervening on his son's behalf. Osorkon's own Chronicle records being expelled and returning, a great rebellion, and reprisals in which enemies were burned alive 'as sacrifice'. The struggle left the Twenty-second Dynasty's authority over Upper Egypt permanently broken.
entries.note: Chronicle of Prince Osorkon: Caminos, The Chronicle of Prince Osorkon (1958). David Aston, 'Takeloth II — A King of the Herakleopolitan/Theban Twenty-Third Dynasty Revisited', in Broekman et al. (eds.), The Libyan Period in Egypt (2009).

entries.label: Piye's conquest of Egypt
entries.hint: Tefnakht of Sais had brought the Delta and much of Middle Egypt under his lead and laid siege to Herakleopolis, Piye's ally. Piye's army, then Piye himself, came down the river: Hermopolis was starved into surrender, the fortified river-port of Memphis stormed from the water, and one by one the northern kings and chiefs came to submit — though the fully royal ones, being ritually impure, were made to stay outside the palace gate. Piye then sailed home to Napata, and northern Egypt slid back toward autonomy.
entries.note: Piye Victory Stela (Cairo JE 48862): Grimal (1981); Lichtheim, AEL III (1980) pp.66–84. Date c.727 (or slightly earlier) per the stela's Year 21. Morkot, The Black Pharaohs (2000) pp.167–201.

entries.label: Assyria invades and sacks Thebes
entries.hint: Esarhaddon of Assyria was thrown back from Egypt in 674 but returned in 671, taking Memphis and carrying Taharqa's queen, heir and court to Nineveh. Taharqa recovered the city; Ashurbanipal reconquered it in 667 and installed local vassals, chief among them Necho I of Sais. When Tantamani killed Necho and retook Memphis in 664, Ashurbanipal came back and in 663 stormed and stripped Thebes itself — carrying off two obelisks and treasure 'beyond counting', an act still remembered by the prophet Nahum.
entries.note: Esarhaddon: the Zincirli and Nahr el-Kalb stelae; Leichty, The Royal Inscriptions of Esarhaddon (2011). Ashurbanipal and the sack of Thebes: Rassam Cylinder / Prism A; Onasch, Die assyrischen Eroberungen Ägyptens (1994); Nahum 3:8–10.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The state contracts — the High Priesthood of Amun as a kingship, the God's Wife of Amun, and rule through Libyan chiefdoms

entries.label: Government by oracle at Thebes
entries.hint: Under the priestly regime, the processional image of Amun made the decisions of state. Carried on the shoulders of priests through the temple, the god 'nodded' or drew back in answer to questions read aloud or shown as written alternatives: who should hold an office, whether a land claim was valid, whether an accused man was guilty, whether exiles could come home. Major rulings were carved up as stelae — the Banishment Stela, the recall of the exiles under Menkheperre — as the formal acts of a divine head of state.
entries.note: Banishment Stela (Louvre C 256) and the Maunier / 'Stèle de l'apanage' texts. Jean-Marie Kruchten, Le grand texte oraculaire de Djéhoutymose (1986); J. Černý, 'Egyptian Oracles', in Parker, A Saite Oracle Papyrus (1962). Kitchen, TIP (1996) §43–58.

entries.label: The High Priesthood of Amun as a state office
entries.hint: At Thebes the High Priest of Amun was also, routinely, the army commander of the south and often the viceroy of Kush — a single hereditary office holding religious, military and civil power, passed from father to son and married into the northern royal house. The priesthood controlled the vast temple estates, the Karnak granaries, and what remained of the trade with Nubia, and walled the sacred precinct like a citadel. It was a kingship in all but the name, and sometimes in the name too.
entries.note: Kitchen, The Third Intermediate Period in Egypt (3rd ed. 1996) §1–58; Karl Jansen-Winkeln, 'The Relevance of Genealogical Information for Egyptian Chronology', Ägypten und Levante 16 (2006). Enclosure wall of Menkheperre at Karnak.

entries.label: The God's Wife's household
entries.hint: The God's Wife of Amun governed the Thebaid through a household staffed by powerful stewards — men like Harwa and Akhamenru under the Kushites, whose own tombs in the Asasif are among the largest private monuments of the age. The office itself passed not by birth but by legal adoption: the sitting God's Wife adopted the next, always a princess of whichever dynasty currently claimed Upper Egypt, and the adoption document functioned as a treaty over who controlled the south.
entries.note: Mariam Ayad, God's Wife, God's Servant (2009). Nitocris Adoption Stela (Cairo JE 36327). Steward tombs: TT37 (Harwa), Diethelm Eigner, Die monumentalen Grabbauten der Spätzeit in der thebanischen Nekropole (1984).

entries.label: Rule through Libyan chiefdoms
entries.hint: The Libyan-descended dynasties governed the Delta less as a bureaucracy than as a set of hereditary chiefdoms. Alongside the king, 'Great Chiefs of the Ma' (Meshwesh) and 'Chiefs of the Libu' held Mendes, Sebennytos, Busiris and the western marches as family fiefs, wore the ostrich plume and side-lock of Libyan rank, and recorded long patrilineal genealogies where earlier Egyptians had recorded offices. Power ran along kinship lines, which is why it fragmented so readily.
entries.note: Anthony Leahy, 'The Libyan Period in Egypt: An Essay in Interpretation', Libyan Studies 16 (1985); Robert Ritner, 'Fragmentation and Re-integration in the Third Intermediate Period', in Broekman et al. (eds.), The Libyan Period in Egypt (2009).

entries.label: The tomb-robbery commissions
entries.hint: When systematic looting of the Theban necropolis could no longer be ignored, the vizier Khaemwaset convened formal commissions: officials inspected the royal and noble tombs, arrested suspects named by informers, extracted confessions by beating the feet and hands, and drew up detailed dockets of what had been stolen and how it was divided. Most royal tombs were reported intact — probably a whitewash, since some commissioners were later found to be in on the thefts.
entries.note: The tomb-robbery papyri: Abbott (BM EA 10221), Amherst, Mayer A and B, BM 10052/10403/10068. T. Eric Peet, The Great Tomb-Robberies of the Twentieth Egyptian Dynasty (1930); Peter Vernus, Affairs and Scandals in Ancient Egypt (2003).

entries.label: Stripping the necropolis, closing the village
entries.hint: The Theban priesthood turned tomb-clearance into policy. Commissions under Pinedjem I and his successors opened the royal tombs, took what gold and silver was left back into the treasury, rewrapped the battered mummies of the New Kingdom kings — dockets note the work reign by reign — and moved them for safety into a few group hiding places. Deir el-Medina, its purpose gone, was abandoned; the workmen's descendants lived on inside the walls of Medinet Habu.
entries.note: Reburial dockets on the coffins and wrappings of Seti I, Ramesses II and others: Kitchen, TIP (1996) §40–58. Caches DB320 (found 1871/officially 1881) and KV35 (Loret, 1898). Nicholas Reeves, Valley of the Kings (1990).

entries.label: The Kushite restoration of pharaonic rule
entries.hint: The Kushite kings governed Egypt as self-conscious restorers of the old order: they took the full five-part titulary, revived the vizierate and the classic temple administration, styled themselves protectors of Egyptian religion and maat, and installed trusted Kushites (and their own women in the Theban offices) over a landscape where local Libyan princes were mostly left in place and confirmed. It was rule by legitimacy and religion more than by force, which is why it collapsed when a stronger force arrived.
entries.note: László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997); Robert Morkot, The Black Pharaohs (2000). Kushite officials in Egypt: Jeremy Pope, The Double Kingdom under Taharqo (2014).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Amun's oracular theocracy at Thebes, the royal caches, and the Kushite revival of the old religion

entries.label: The theocracy of Amun
entries.hint: Theban Egypt reorganised itself around the idea that Amun was the actual king. Documents were dated by the god, land was held 'of Amun', the god's oracle appointed officials and settled disputes, and the human High Priest governed explicitly as Amun's agent. The theology that had made Amun the empire's patron now made him, in the Thebaid, the constitutional sovereign — the nearest thing the ancient Near East produced to a formal temple-state.
entries.note: Jan Assmann, The Search for God in Ancient Egypt (2001) pp.145–89; Erik Hornung, Conceptions of God in Ancient Egypt (1982). The 'Direct Rule of Amun': Kitchen, TIP (1996) §43–58.

entries.label: The dead king's body and the portable afterlife
entries.hint: With the royal tombs plundered and the great decorated private tomb no longer affordable or safe, funerary religion moved onto the coffin and the papyrus roll. Bodies were packed and painted to look lifelike, sealed in nested 'yellow' coffins covered edge to edge with protective scenes and spells, and buried in reused family tombs or temple ground with a Book of the Dead and, for the Amun clergy, illustrated 'mythological papyri' of the sun's night journey. The tomb had become something you carried with you.
entries.note: Andrzej Niwiński, 21st Dynasty Coffins from Thebes (1988) and Studies on the Illustrated Theban Funerary Papyri (1989). John H. Taylor, Death and the Afterlife in Ancient Egypt (2001) pp.230–41.

entries.label: The sacred animals move to centre stage
entries.hint: Animal cults, always present, expanded fast in this period. The Apis bulls of Memphis, each the living image of Ptah, began to be buried in a monumental rock-cut gallery at Saqqara, the Serapeum, with royal-scale stone sarcophagi and dated stelae that have become a chronological backbone for the era. Cat burials at the Bubasteion, and the first ibis and falcon catacombs, point to a religion increasingly focused on the animal as a channel to the divine.
entries.note: Serapeum: Auguste Mariette, Le Sérapéum de Memphis (1857–66); the Apis stelae, Malinine, Posener & Vercoutter, Catalogue des stèles du Sérapéum (1968). Dorothy Kessler & Salima Ikram on the animal necropoleis.

entries.label: The Kushite revival of Amun
entries.hint: The Napatan kings were fervent devotees of Amun in his Nubian home under the pinnacle of Gebel Barkal, which they treated as a second Karnak and the true origin of the god. They rebuilt temples the length of their domain, observed Egyptian purity rules more strictly than Egyptians did, travelled the length of the Nile to be crowned at both Napata and Thebes, and consciously modelled their art and texts on the Old and Middle Kingdoms — a foreign dynasty presenting itself as more authentically Egyptian than the Egyptians.
entries.note: Timothy Kendall, 'Gebel Barkal and Ancient Napata', and the Boston/Sudan mission reports. Coronation journey: the Kushite enthronement stelae (Aspelta, and earlier). Donald Redford, From Slave to Pharaoh (2004) pp.109–41.

entries.label: The Memphite Theology and the recovery of old texts
entries.hint: A basalt slab set up by Shabaka in the temple of Ptah at Memphis states that the king found a worm-eaten papyrus of an ancestral work and had it re-cut in stone. Its text has Ptah create the world by conceiving it in his heart and speaking it — a theology of creation by thought and word. Whether the original was truly ancient or a fresh composition dressed as one, the gesture is typical of the age's antiquarianism: authority now lay in recovering, or claiming to recover, the deep past.
entries.note: Shabaka Stone (BM EA 498): Breasted, 'The Philosophy of a Memphite Priest', ZÄS 39 (1901); Friedrich Junge, 'Zur Fehldatierung des sog. Denkmals memphitischer Theologie', MDAIK 29 (1973) argues for a Kushite-era composition.

entries.label: Amulets, oracles and the protective gods
entries.hint: In insecure times ordinary religion turned more protective. People wore more and denser amulets, carried little 'oracular amuletic decrees' — papyrus strips in which a god promises in the first person to guard the bearer from named dangers — sought cures by sleeping in temple precincts, and poured water over Horus-on-the-crocodiles healing stelae to drink the runoff against scorpion and snake bite. The household gods Bes and the dwarf-form Ptah-Pataikos were everywhere.
entries.note: Oracular Amuletic Decrees: I.E.S. Edwards, Hieratic Papyri in the British Museum, Fourth Series: Oracular Amuletic Decrees (1960). Horus cippi: Heike Sternberg-el Hotabi, Untersuchungen zur Überlieferungsgeschichte der Horusstelen (1999).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Medinet Habu, the silver coffins of Tanis, bronze statuary, and the archaising art of the Kushite court

entries.label: Medinet Habu
entries.hint: Ramesses III's mortuary temple, set inside a fortified enclosure with a Syrian-style fortified gatehouse, is the best-preserved large temple of the New Kingdom and the last built on that scale for centuries. Its outer walls carry the fullest surviving battle reliefs in Egypt — the Libyan wars and the land and sea fights against the Sea Peoples — and a great calendar listing every festival of the year with its offerings. When Thebes fell apart, the temple's walls became the town.
entries.note: Epigraphic Survey (Oriental Institute), Medinet Habu, 9 vols. (1930–2009). Uvo Hölscher, The Excavation of Medinet Habu (1934–54). The festival calendar: Harold Nelson and the Survey volumes.

entries.label: The Report of Wenamun
entries.hint: An envoy of the Karnak temple is sent to Byblos to buy cedar for Amun's ceremonial barque. He is robbed at Dor, kept waiting for months, and finally told to his face by the prince of Byblos that Egypt no longer commands anything for free — 'I am not your servant, nor the servant of him who sent you'. Whether an actual dispatch or a polished literary fiction, its wry first-person voice and its picture of a shrunken Egypt make it the outstanding prose work of the age.
entries.note: P. Moscow 120: Gardiner, Late-Egyptian Stories (1932); Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976) pp.224–30. On genre: Bernd Ulrich Schipper, Die Erzählung des Wenamun (2005).

entries.label: The silver kings of Tanis
entries.hint: The undisturbed royal tombs Pierre Montet found inside the Tanis temple precinct in 1939–40 held goldsmiths' work to rival Tutankhamun's, but almost unknown because of the timing. Psusennes I lay in a coffin of solid silver — a metal rarer than gold in Egypt — under a gold face mask; his general Wendjebauendjed had a gold mask of his own; and Shoshenq II was found in a falcon-headed coffin of silver. In an age of looted valuables, Tanis is where the era's decorative art survives.
entries.note: Montet, La nécropole royale de Tanis, 3 vols. (1947–60). Exhibition catalogue: Gold of the Pharaohs: 3,000 Years of Ancient Egyptian Goldsmithing (Bonn/Paris, 2021).

entries.label: The age of bronze statuary
entries.hint: Third Intermediate Period sculptors did their finest work in cast bronze: hollow figures of gods and of temple donors, often inlaid with gold, silver and electrum wire and sheet. The statuette of the God's Wife Karomama, its garments picked out in gold and electrum damascening, and the inlaid bronze of the 'Lady Takushit' are the masterpieces. Temples filled with such votive bronzes, a democratised form of dedication as royal stone monuments grew rarer.
entries.note: Karomama statuette (Louvre N 500): Christiane Ziegler, various. Takushit (Athens, National Archaeological Museum). Technique: Marsha Hill (ed.), Gifts for the Gods: Images from Egyptian Temples (2007).

entries.label: The archaising turn
entries.hint: Kushite and early Saite artists deliberately reached back over a millennium for their models. Relief in the huge new tomb-chapels of the Asasif copies Old Kingdom agricultural and offering scenes and Eighteenth-Dynasty compositions; sculptors revived Middle Kingdom facial types; texts long out of use were recopied. It was not a failure of invention but a programme — anchoring a broken present to the authority of the classic past.
entries.note: Asasif tombs of Harwa (TT37), Karakhamun (TT223), Montuemhat (TT34): Eigner, Die monumentalen Grabbauten der Spätzeit (1984). Archaism: Peter Der Manuelian, Living in the Past: Studies in Archaism of the Egyptian Twenty-Sixth Dynasty (1994).

entries.label: The Kushite royal image
entries.hint: The Kushite pharaohs invented their own royal iconography: a close-fitting cap-crown, two rearing cobras at the brow instead of one, and a cord necklace with ram's-head amulets of Amun. Their portrait sculpture — the granite heads of Taharqa and Shabaka — is broad-featured, powerfully modelled and markedly un-idealised. They also revived the royal pyramid, small and steep-sided, for their own burials at el-Kurru and Nuri, a form Egypt itself had abandoned 800 years earlier.
entries.note: Kushite regalia: László Török, The Image of the Ordered World in Ancient Nubian Art (2002). El-Kurru and Nuri pyramids: Dows Dunham, The Royal Cemeteries of Kush I–II (1950–55). Sculpture: Edna Russmann, The Representation of the King in the XXVth Dynasty (1974).

entries.label: The chantress and the temple choir
entries.hint: Temple music became a mass institution. The title 'chantress (shemayet) of Amun' — a woman who shook the sistrum and sang in the god's service — spread from a small elite to something close to a general marker of respectable married women on Theban coffins and stelae. The God's Wife of Amun maintained her own body of female musicians, and the sistrum and the beaded menit necklace, both associated with Hathor, are the instruments shown again and again in the period's art.
entries.note: Lise Manniche, Music and Musicians in Ancient Egypt (1991); Suzanne Onstine, The Role of the Chantress (Šmˁyt) in Ancient Egypt (2005). Emily Teeter, Music and Musicians in Ancient Egypt (Oriental Institute).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The onomastica, the tomb-robbery inquiries, the temple libraries, and the Kushite return to the Pyramid Texts

entries.label: The temple as archive and House of Life
entries.hint: As the palace's reach shrank, the temples became the country's memory. Their scriptoria, the 'Houses of Life', copied, corrected and canonised religious, medical and ritual texts; their libraries held the master copies (a book-list survives, later, on a wall at Edfu); and their priesthoods were now the people who could read the old scripts and knew the old rites. Egyptian learning in this period is temple learning, curated by a hereditary clergy.
entries.note: Alan Gardiner, 'The House of Life', JEA 24 (1938). Temple libraries: the Edfu catalogue (Ptolemaic but reflecting long practice). Kim Ryholt & Gojko Barjamovic (eds.), Libraries before Alexandria (2019).

entries.label: Genealogy as scholarship
entries.hint: Where earlier Egyptians defined themselves by office, the Libyan-period elite defined themselves by descent, and recording it became a discipline. A statue of a Memphite priest carries his paternal line back some sixty generations, roughly a thousand years; the Pasenhor stela traces the ruling house to a Libyan ancestor fifteen generations back. These constructed lineages were both legitimation and a genuine effort to bridge the documentary gap left by the collapse.
entries.note: The 'Berlin genealogy' of the Memphite priests (Berlin ÄM 23673): Borchardt, Die Mittel zur zeitlichen Festlegung von Punkten der ägyptischen Geschichte (1935). Pasenhor / Serapeum Stela 31 (Louvre): Malinine et al., Catalogue des stèles du Sérapéum (1968); Kitchen, TIP (1996) §183–90.

entries.label: The great surveys and the inquiry method
entries.hint: Even in decline the Egyptian state produced formidable paperwork. The Wilbour Papyrus is a field-by-field cadastral survey of some 150 kilometres of Middle Egypt, recording who held each plot, from which institution, and its assessed yield — the most detailed land document to survive from the ancient world. The Turin Mining Papyrus maps the Wadi Hammamat quarry district in plan and section. The tomb-robbery commissions applied a repeatable procedure of inspection, testimony and inventory.
entries.note: Wilbour Papyrus: Alan Gardiner, The Wilbour Papyrus, 4 vols. (1941–52). Turin Mining Papyrus: Harrell & Brown, JARCE 29 (1992). Sally Katary, Land Tenure in the Ramesside Period (1989).

entries.label: The Brooklyn snakebite papyrus
entries.hint: A papyrus now in Brooklyn, of Late Period date but drawing on older material, is a systematic manual of snakes and their bites: the first section describes around forty snakes by colour, markings and habits, names the god each is sacred to, and rates each bite as fatal, treatable or minor; the second gives treatments. It is effectively an ancient work of applied herpetology, and modern zoologists have identified many of its species.
entries.note: Brooklyn Papyri 47.218.48 and 47.218.85: Serge Sauneron, Un traité égyptien d'ophiologie (1989). Species identifications: Warrell, in Nunn, Ancient Egyptian Medicine (1996) pp.190–91.

entries.label: The revival of the Pyramid Texts
entries.hint: Kushite-era scholars went looking, in temple libraries and on Old Kingdom monuments, for the oldest funerary literature they could find, and put it back into use. The tomb of the priest Karakhamun in the Asasif carries long extracts of the Pyramid Texts, first composed around 2350 BC and unused for well over a millennium, alongside Coffin Texts and Book of the Dead spells — a deliberate act of textual archaeology that the Saite tombs then took further.
entries.note: Tomb of Karakhamun (TT223): the South Asasif Conservation Project (Elena Pischikova). Pyramid Text revival: Harold Hays & others; Der Manuelian, Living in the Past (1994) pp.1–12.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The failure of the grain state, the tomb-robbery economy, the temple as banker, and Kushite gold

entries.label: The failure of the redistributive state
entries.hint: The New Kingdom economy of state granaries paying fixed rations broke down under the later Ramessides. The tomb-workers' grain came weeks or months late, forcing the first recorded strikes; the price of emmer on the Theban market rose to several times its long-standing level during a subsistence crisis and only slowly fell; and officials were caught diverting temple grain. The machine that had fed the imperial state could no longer reliably feed a single village.
entries.note: Turin Strike Papyrus: Edgerton, JNES 10 (1951); Paul Frandsen, 'Editing Reality: The Turin Strike Papyrus', in Israelit-Groll (ed.), Studies in Egyptology (1990). Prices: Jac. Janssen, Commodity Prices from the Ramessid Period (1975).

entries.label: The tomb-robbery economy
entries.hint: With no new gold coming from a lost empire, the metal already in Egypt was recycled — much of it out of the tombs. Organised gangs stripped royal and private burials, melted the gold on the spot, and passed it through fences and complicit officials; the trial records track exact shares. Then the state took over the practice: the Theban priesthood's own commissions emptied the royal tombs of their remaining precious metal and returned it to the treasury.
entries.note: Tomb-robbery papyri: Peet, The Great Tomb-Robberies of the Twentieth Egyptian Dynasty (1930). The state 'restoration' as asset-stripping: Reeves, Valley of the Kings (1990) pp.276–82; Kitchen, TIP (1996) §40–58.

entries.label: The temple as landlord and banker
entries.hint: With the crown weak, the temples were the durable economic institution. The Wilbour Papyrus shows the temple of Amun and other religious houses holding much of the surveyed farmland of Middle Egypt, worked by tenants who paid a share to the god's estate. Temples also stored grain against shortage, advanced seed and goods at interest, and held valuables on deposit — functions that in a coinless economy made them the nearest thing to banks.
entries.note: Wilbour Papyrus: Gardiner, The Wilbour Papyrus (1941–52); Sally Katary, Land Tenure in the Ramesside Period (1989). Temple economy: Barry Kemp, Ancient Egypt: Anatomy of a Civilization (2006) pp.248–60.

entries.label: The end of empire income
entries.hint: Egypt's New Kingdom budget had rested on Nubian gold and Levantine tribute. When Nubia went its own way after Ramesses XI and the last Asian holdings were gone, both revenue streams stopped, and the state was thrown back on the produce of the Nile valley alone. The clearest measure is monumental building: after Medinet Habu, no king for three centuries could raise anything remotely comparable, and even temple additions became modest.
entries.note: On the fiscal contraction: Warburton, State and Economy in Ancient Egypt (1997); Kitchen, TIP (1996), passim on the scale of Twenty-first- and Twenty-second-Dynasty building versus the New Kingdom.

entries.label: Kushite gold and the reunited Nile
entries.hint: The Kushite conquest reconnected Egypt to the goldfields of Nubia and the desert, and to the Red Sea and inner-African routes that fed Napata. Taharqa's building programme — the largest since the New Kingdom, at Karnak, Kawa, Sanam, Gebel Barkal and in the Nubian temples — is the visible return on that reunification. The economic case for a Kushite Egypt, as much as the religious one, was access to wealth Egypt alone had lost.
entries.note: Kawa temple building accounts of Taharqa: Macadam, The Temples of Kawa I (1949). Nubian gold: László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997) pp.388–408; the Kushite economy, Jeremy Pope, The Double Kingdom under Taharqo (2014).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The spread of iron, mummification at its technical peak, and the bronze-casters' craft

entries.label: Iron becomes a working metal
entries.hint: Over these centuries iron shifted in Egypt from a rare curiosity to an ordinary material for tools and weapons — chisels, knives, arrowheads and spearpoints turn up in Twentieth- to Twenty-fifth-Dynasty contexts. Egypt was a slow, partial adopter: it had little workable ore, imported much of its iron, and kept using bronze alongside. The Assyrians who invaded in the 670s–660s came with a fully iron-armed army, a technological as well as a numerical edge.
entries.note: Jane Waldbaum, From Bronze to Iron (1978); Ogden, 'Metals', in Nicholson & Shaw (eds.), Ancient Egyptian Materials and Technology (2000) pp.166–68. Assyrian ironworking: overview in Cline, 1177 B.C. (2014).

entries.label: Embalming at its technical peak
entries.hint: The Twenty-first-Dynasty embalmers of Thebes reached the highest technical standard the craft ever attained. They packed the emptied body cavity and, through small incisions, the limbs and face with linen, sawdust and mud to restore a lifelike fullness; inserted artificial eyes; painted the skin (red for men, yellow for women); and returned the treated internal organs to the body in packages. The mummies of the priestly families are strikingly true to life. Standards then fell away over the following centuries.
entries.note: A. Rosalie David, The Manchester Mummy Project and Egyptian Mummies (2000); Bob Brier & Ronald Wade, on reconstructing the technique. The priestly-cache mummies: Smith, The Royal Mummies (1912); the Bab el-Gasus find (1891).

entries.label: The cartonnage industry
entries.hint: With decorated tombs no longer the norm, protection for the dead was built into the coffin. Workshops turned out nested sets of wooden 'yellow' coffins painted edge to edge with spells and vignettes, and moulded cases of glued linen and plaster (cartonnage) fitted over the wrapped body and gessoed and painted. Made to a repertoire of stock scenes with the owner's name and titles filled in, they are effectively a mass-production line for the afterlife.
entries.note: John H. Taylor, Coffins as Evidence for a North-South Divide, in Broekman et al. (eds.), The Libyan Period in Egypt (2009); Niwiński, 21st Dynasty Coffins from Thebes (1988). Cartonnage technique: Taylor, Death and the Afterlife in Ancient Egypt (2001).

entries.label: Hollow-casting and precious-metal inlay
entries.hint: The period's signature craft was fine bronzeworking. Founders cast large figures hollow around a core by the lost-wax method, and decorators cut fine channels into the finished surface and hammered in gold, silver and electrum wire and sheet to render garments, feathers and inscriptions — the damascening seen on the Karomama statuette. Temple courts filled with these votive bronzes as the stone monument became a rarer luxury.
entries.note: Marsha Hill & Deborah Schorsch (eds.), Gifts for the Gods: Images from Egyptian Temples (2007); Schorsch, 'Precious-metal polychromy in Egypt in the time of Tutankhamun', JEA 87 (2001). Karomama (Louvre N 500).

entries.label: The fortified gate and the defensive town
entries.hint: An age of raids and civil war built for defence. Ramesses III fronted his temple with a migdol — a tall twin-towered gatehouse copied from Syrian fortress design — and the great temple enclosures at Karnak and elsewhere were walled like citadels, sometimes sheltering whole populations. In the Delta, Libyan and later Kushite rulers held fortified towns, and the Kushites built a chain of fortresses to hold Lower Nubia.
entries.note: The Medinet Habu migdol: Hölscher, The Excavation of Medinet Habu (1934–54). Third Intermediate Period fortified settlement: Kate Spence and others on Delta 'temple-towns'; Kushite fortresses, David O'Connor, Ancient Nubia (1993).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Report of Wenamun, the Libyan and Meshwesh settlement, Phoenician trade, and the Kushite reunion of the Nile

entries.label: The Libyan settlement of the Delta
entries.hint: The Libyan groups Ramesses III defeated kept coming — as war captives settled in military colonies, as mercenaries paid in land, and as free migrants — until people of Libyan descent held much of the Delta's land and its local chieftaincies. Within two centuries their leaders were kings of Egypt. It is one of history's clearest cases of a territory taken over by sustained migration and military settlement rather than by conquest.
entries.note: Anthony Leahy (ed.), Libya and Egypt c.1300–750 BC (1990); Leahy, 'The Libyan Period in Egypt', Libyan Studies 16 (1985); Robert Ritner, 'Libyan vs. Nubian as the Ideal Egyptian', in Cohen et al. (eds.), Egypt and the Egyptians (2009).

entries.label: The Phoenicians carry the trade
entries.hint: As Egyptian ships stopped sailing the Mediterranean, the cities of the Lebanese coast took over the sea lanes. Wenamun has to buy his cedar from a Byblos that no longer owes Egypt anything; over the following centuries Phoenician traders spread Egyptian and Egyptianising objects — scarabs, amulets, ivories, faience — as far as Carthage, Sardinia and southern Spain, making 'Egypt' a style available across the Mediterranean without Egyptian involvement.
entries.note: Report of Wenamun (see Expression). Phoenician aegyptiaca: Günther Hölbl, Ägyptisches Kulturgut im phönikischen und punischen Sardinien (1986); Christoph Uehlinger, and the wider 'orientalizing' literature.

entries.label: Egypt among the kingdoms of the Levant
entries.hint: A weakened Egypt was still a Levantine actor. Shoshenq I raided Judah and Israel; the rebel Jeroboam sheltered in Egypt before founding the northern kingdom; late Twenty-first-Dynasty tradition has a pharaoh's daughter married to Solomon; and in the 700s Egyptian and then Kushite kings encouraged the small states to resist Assyria, promising help that too often failed to arrive — 'that broken reed of a staff, Egypt', in the Assyrian taunt.
entries.note: 1 Kings 11–14; 2 Kings 17–19 / Isaiah 36. Kitchen, TIP (1996) §251–74; Bernd Schipper, Israel und Ägypten in der Königszeit (1999). The 'broken reed': 2 Kings 18:21.

entries.label: The Kushite reunion of the Nile
entries.hint: For the first time since the New Kingdom collapsed, one state ran the Nile from the Delta to beyond the Fourth Cataract. Under the Kushite pharaohs, people, goods, art styles and cults moved freely along the whole river again: Kushite princes and princesses held Egyptian offices at Thebes and Memphis, Egyptian priests and craftsmen worked at Napata and Kawa, and Nubian and Egyptian religion fused around Amun. Scholars call it the 'double kingdom'.
entries.note: Jeremy Pope, The Double Kingdom under Taharqo: Studies in the History of Kush and Egypt (2014); László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997) pp.143–88; Robert Morkot, The Black Pharaohs (2000).

entries.label: Assyria enters Egypt
entries.hint: The confrontation with Assyria ran from a distant contingent at Qarqar in 853 to Assyrian armies on the Nile a century and a half later. Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal took Memphis and Thebes, deported the Kushite royal family and Egyptian notables to Nineveh, installed a network of local Egyptian vassals bound by loyalty oaths, and hauled off obelisks and treasure. It is the first time a Mesopotamian empire ruled part of Egypt, and it broke the Kushite hold for good.
entries.note: Leichty, The Royal Inscriptions of Esarhaddon (2011); Ashurbanipal's Prism A/Rassam Cylinder. Onasch, Die assyrischen Eroberungen Ägyptens (1994); Anthony Spalinger, 'Assurbanipal and Egypt', JAOS 94 (1974).

entries.label: Ionians and Carians appear on the coast
entries.hint: In the seventh century Greek and Carian ships — traders and raiders both — began working the Egyptian coast. Herodotus tells how 'bronze men from the sea', Ionian and Carian pirates driven ashore, were taken into Egyptian service by Psamtik I of Sais, right at the close of this period, and helped him win control of Egypt. Their arrival is the beginning of the sustained Greek presence that the Saite kings would build on with the trading colony at Naukratis.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.152, 2.154. Alan Lloyd, Herodotus Book II: Commentary (1988); Alexandra Villing & Udo Schlotzhauer (eds.), Naukratis: Greek Diversity in Egypt (2006).
